description: A junior-year CS student with a strong background in theoretical data structures and high-level application development who feels mathematically confident but technically intimidated by the shift to C-based systems programming.

nodes.description: Introduction to C programming syntax, pointers, and memory management essential for systems work.
nodes.title: C Foundations for Systems Programming
nodes.personalizationRationale: Because the student has no_prior_exposure to systems programming, this node builds the necessary C-language foundation for understanding OS kernels.

nodes.description: Overview of CPU registers, the fetch-decode-execute cycle, and how interrupts bridge hardware and software.
nodes.personalizationRationale: As a student with no_prior_exposure, grasping the underlying hardware architecture is a prerequisite for understanding OS structures.
nodes.title: Hardware-Software Interface Overview

nodes.description: Deep dive into the transition between User Mode and Kernel Mode using system calls.
nodes.title: The System Call Mechanism
nodes.personalizationRationale: Providing extra context on the privilege separation for a student with no_prior_exposure ensures they understand the fundamental security model of an OS.
This core node provides the essential syllabus coverage of OS services required for all students regardless of background.
nodes.title: OS Structures & Services
nodes.description: Introduction to OS services, system structures, and the difference between monolithic and microkernel designs.

nodes.title: The Process Abstraction
nodes.personalizationRationale: Understanding the process abstraction is fundamental to the entire course; this node ensures the student masters lifecycle management.
nodes.description: Detailed look at process states, the Process Control Block (PCB), and context switching.
Mechanisms for processes to communicate via shared memory, message passing, and sockets.
nodes.personalizationRationale: IPC is a core syllabus requirement that bridges process management with distributed and concurrent systems.
nodes.title: Inter-Process Communication (IPC)

nodes.description: Exploring multithreading models, threading libraries (Pthreads/Windows), and implicit threading.
nodes.title: Threads & Threading Models
nodes.personalizationRationale: Thread management is a core requirement; even with no_prior_exposure, the student must master concurrent execution units.

nodes.description: Analysis of CPU scheduling algorithms including FCFS, SJF, Priority, and Round Robin.
nodes.personalizationRationale: Mastering scheduling criteria and algorithms is a core competency tested on both the midterm and final exams.
nodes.title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms
Midterm Review (Ch. 1-5)
nodes.personalizationRationale: This required assessment checkpoint prepares students for the midterm, ensuring no_prior_exposure doesn't lead to early exam failure.
nodes.description: Comprehensive review session covering Chapters 1-5 in preparation for the week-8 midterm exam.
The critical-section problem and software/hardware solutions including Mutex locks.
nodes.personalizationRationale: Synchronization is a core course objective; this node builds the tools needed for safe concurrent programming.
nodes.title: Process Synchronization: Mutexes
Semaphores & Classic Sync Problems
nodes.personalizationRationale: Classic synchronization problems are required syllabus components and are heavily used in upcoming project deliveries.
nodes.description: Using semaphores and monitors to solve classic problems like Bounded Buffer and Dining Philosophers.
Characterizing deadlock and applying prevention, avoidance, and detection strategies.
nodes.title: Deadlock Prevention & Avoidance
nodes.personalizationRationale: Deadlock theory is a mandatory module required for modeling system reliability analytically.

nodes.title: Physical Memory & Paging
nodes.personalizationRationale: Core memory management concepts are essential for the final exam and the memory-related programming projects.
nodes.description: Logical vs physical addressing, contiguous allocation, and the transition to paging.
Demand paging, page replacement algorithms (LRU, Optimal), and the mechanics of thrashing.
nodes.title: Virtual Memory & Page Replacement
nodes.personalizationRationale: Virtual memory management is a mandatory block that explains how OS handles resources larger than physical RAM.

nodes.title: I/O Systems & Interfaces
nodes.personalizationRationale: I/O systems are a required capstone topic to understand how the OS interacts with external devices.
nodes.description: Understanding I/O hardware, polling vs interrupts, and DMA interfaces.

nodes.personalizationRationale: File system implementation is a core requirement that combines memory management and I/O concepts.
nodes.title: File System Implementation
nodes.description: Structure of file systems, directory implementation, and allocation methods (linked, indexed).
Cumulative review of the entire syllabus (Ch. 1-15) in preparation for the week-17 final exam.
nodes.title: Cumulative Final Review
nodes.personalizationRationale: Final assessment checkpoint to ensure the student has successfully bridged their no_prior_exposure gap to master the full syllabus.
